rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2-3, two-year (2012-2013) field experiment at Bushland TX comparing plant-feedback (IRT wireless sensor network) VRI scheduling with manual neutron-probe scheduling on cotton. Q2: Table 2 and Table 3, Section 3.2-3.3, own measurements of post-plant irrigation amounts, ETc (soil water balance), WUE and IWUE under sensor-based scheduling at 75/50/25% deficit levels; WUE and IWUE were similar between methods within a level, sensor plots at I50/I25 received 15-120% more irrigation. Q4: Section 3.2 and Appendix Figs A.1-A.2, neutron-probe soil water profiles measured, authors report storage at 30-110 cm and no deep percolation or runoff; iCWSI values per plot computed (Fig 4a) and ETc derived from soil water balance. Q7: Abstract and Section 4, authors state the system could be used for site-specific control at the higher irrigation levels (I75, I50) and that excess irrigation early in the season arose from soil background with low canopy cover (NDVI<0.25 data excluded). Q8: Section 3.3, solenoid valves wired in reverse in 2013 so only 3 replications used; false positive triggers under partial canopy; greater SD in plant-feedback plots requiring MBR refinements; failure to maintain the 25% deficit level. Q9: Tables 2 and 3 report means <U+00B1> standard deviation for irrigation amounts, lint yield, ETc, WUE and IWUE.
rows.notes: Direction only partly matches the claim: the study does not show increased CWP or water saving relative to the comparator; WUE/IWUE were similar between methods and the sensor-based system applied equal or more water (twice at I25). Support is for feasibility of sensor-based deficit irrigation at I75/I50 without yield or WUE loss, not for increased CWP. Comparator is research-station neutron-probe scheduling, not typical farmer practice. Q7 is a judgement call: applicability only at higher irrigation levels is stated in abstract and conclusions. Single site, single soil, single crop, half a center pivot field.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2-3, two-year field experiment (2012, 2013) with randomized complete block design, four replications, measuring cotton lint yield under plant-feedback (iCWSI) versus manual neutron-probe scheduling. Q2: Table 3 and Section 3.3, hand-harvested lint yields; similar between methods at I75 (181 vs 182 g m-2 in 2012) and I50, significantly greater for plant feedback at I25 (142 vs 92 g m-2) but with twice the irrigation; overall method mean yield higher for plant feedback in both years. Q4: Section 3.3 and Table A.2, ETc from neutron-probe soil water balance, boll number and boll weight per plant measured, linear yield-ETc relations reported (r2 0.95-0.96), yield differences attributed to greater irrigation amounts; iCWSI per plot (Fig 4a). Q7: Abstract and Section 4, authors state the system can control site-specific irrigation for cotton at higher irrigation levels (I75, I50) and that low early-season canopy cover produced false positive triggers; further research needed to maintain the 25% level. Q8: Section 3.3 and 4, 2013 valve mis-wiring reduced analysis to 21 plots (3 replications); higher yield SD in plant-feedback plots; false positive triggers with partial canopy; threshold for I25 needs adjustment. Q9: Table 3 reports lint yield means <U+00B1> standard deviation for each method <U+00D7> level combination.
rows.notes: Study supports yields equal to (not greater than) manual neutron-probe scheduling at I75 and I50; the higher yield at I25 came from double the irrigation, so it does not demonstrate yield gain from well-regulated deficit irrigation. Comparator is a research scheduling method rather than current farmer practice. Single site, soil and crop; plot scale within one center pivot field. Q7 rated yes on the basis of the stated restriction to higher irrigation levels; some doubt whether this is a requirement or a finding of variation.

notes: Full text appears complete including appendix. Study is a primary two-year field experiment on IRT-based plant feedback VRI scheduling of cotton at one USDA-ARS site; both claim rows cite it for increases in CWP and yield that the study only partly supports (parity, not improvement, at moderate deficit levels).
